stories.headline: Starship Flight 15 reaches orbit, deploys 26 Starlink V3 satellites, and Ship 42 stays healthy overhead
stories.why_read: Last night your timeline was wall-to-wall Starship, and for good reason: this is the second orbital Starship flight and the first that carried a real operational payload.
body: SpaceX launched the 15th Starship test from Starbase on November 13, reaching orbit and deploying 26 Starlink V3 satellites, according to a summary of posts on X. Super Heavy Booster 22 separated with hot staging, but the planned tower catch was called off for safety and the booster was sent to a landing burn and splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico instead. SpaceX later posted that Starship and its heatshield were healthy as the vehicle kept circling Earth.

The ship's long stay in orbit is the interesting part. Reports describe a potential catch attempt for Ship 42 roughly a day after liftoff, which would be the first time an upper stage that has been to orbit comes home to the tower. Farzad's explainer on why the ship circles Earth 14 times before returning is a good companion read if you want the orbital mechanics behind the timing.

stories.headline: Grok Bot now joins Zoom, Google Meet and Teams calls as a live participant
stories.why_read: You run a fleet of bots already; this turns them from chat-only helpers into colleagues who can sit in the meeting, take notes and follow up.
body: Grok Bot can now enter video meetings on Zoom, Google Meet and Microsoft Teams, where it transcribes in real time, answers in chat, tracks decisions and sends a summary with action items afterwards, according to a summary of posts on X. You paste a meeting link into a chat with a bot, approve it, and the host admits it. Bots connected to a calendar can join on their own on paid Team, Enterprise and Ultra plans.

Cursor CEO Michael Truell, in a post you bookmarked, put it bluntly: within a couple of quarters it will be normal for work meetings to include bots, and this early beta is a rough first glimpse. Early users report bots sitting through dozens of meetings on their own and getting more useful as they gather context.

stories.headline: A router overload freezes U.S. air traffic: FAA nationwide ground stop lasts more than four hours
stories.why_read: A textbook systems failure: legacy network gear got overloaded, radar and comms data became unreliable, and the only safe option was to stop the whole country.
body: The FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop for departing flights at 3:54 p.m. ET on Friday and lifted it at 8:15 p.m. ET, NBC News reports, after more than 7,000 flights were canceled. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed an outdated air traffic control system in which routers "got overloaded with data," causing instability in radar and communications across centers and TRACONs. He said the instability was detected at 3:36 p.m. and that the FAA never lost all telecom or radar, so the stop was precautionary. Homeland Security said there was no sign of a cyberattack.

The timing drew skepticism online because the FAA had finished rolling out its AI-assisted SMART airspace tool just days earlier; Duffy and the developer say it played no role. The knock-on effects spread: Amtrak's booking system buckled under a surge of stranded travelers Friday evening, and Hawaii's transportation department briefly blamed SpaceX debris before the real cause was clear. Duffy says the system should catch up before the Thanksgiving rush.

stories.headline: Tesla opens Cybercab orders to select customers at $29,990, with a $299 monthly autonomy subscription
stories.why_read: The car with no steering wheel or pedals is now something an individual can order, which even longtime skeptics on your timeline are conceding.
body: Select Tesla customers received invites on November 13 to order the two-seat Cybercab for personal use at $29,990, with a $1,000 deposit and a required $299-a-month Autonomy Subscription, according to a summary of posts on X. Deliveries are slated for December 2026 in Austin. The car runs only inside limited Texas Robotaxi zones for personal trips, with no ridesharing allowed, and owners handle insurance and charging.

Elon Musk said nationwide expansion waits on regulators and hinted the subscription is priced too high. Farzad, in a post you reposted, formally retracted his bet that Tesla would add a steering wheel and pedals. For Austin residents, this is the first chance to own one of these cars outright rather than just hail one.

stories.headline: WSJ: Nvidia funded small clouds to buy its GPUs and keep demand looking hot, over its CFO's objections
stories.why_read: The Huang story is shifting from personal scandal to business practice, and this is the thread that matters to anyone pricing GPU capacity.
body: Following Jensen Huang's exit, a Wall Street Journal report (summarized by TechPowerUp via Wccftech) alleges Nvidia invested in AI startups and small cloud providers that then bought its GPUs and built data centers, helping sustain the look of red-hot demand while it worked through a large supply commitment from TSMC. The report describes an August meeting where Colette Kress, then CFO and now acting CEO, pushed to cut back circular financing, including the $250 billion OpenAI deal, and Huang allegedly called her a "deer in the headlights."

Kress's concern, per the report, was that many of those smaller clouds could not actually afford the GPUs, making them a possible financial dead end. The move came as hyperscalers shifted toward custom silicon. These are allegations from one report, but together with this week's disclosures about ballooning financing guarantees, they frame the questions Nvidia's first earnings call without Huang will have to answer.

stories.headline: ggml, the tensor library under llama.cpp, ships v1.0.0 with FP8 support and a pruned API
stories.why_read: The engine that makes local LLMs run on laptops just declared itself stable, and the backend list reads like a tour of every accelerator you own.
body: ggml 1.0.0 removes the deprecated public API and the legacy DIAG_MASK ops, adds configurable YaRN truncation and OCP FP8 support, and bumps the RPC protocol to v9 with faster loading and graceful failure on unreachable peers, according to the release notes. The scheduler now skips uploading inputs that are never read, and the MoE cache can compute some cache misses on the CPU asynchronously.

Backend work is broad: few-row quantized matmuls and MoE fusion on CUDA and Metal, fused NVFP4 gate/up matmuls, a Vulkan prefill FlashAttention path, a device-side MoE scheduler on SYCL, FlashAttention for Adreno via OpenCL, new WebGPU kernels and more Hexagon op coverage. If you build on llama.cpp, expect the RPC version bump to reject older peers.

stories.headline: One Starship flight added up to 26 terabits per second to Starlink, and V4 is already on the drawing board
stories.why_read: This is the economic case for Starship in one number: a single flight carried the bandwidth of about ten Falcon 9 Starlink launches.
body: The 26 Starlink V3 satellites on Flight 15 add up to 26 Tbps of capacity, roughly equal to ten Falcon 9 launches of earlier models, according to a summary of posts on X and Starlink's own post, which you reposted. Each V3 satellite is described as carrying about 1 Tbps of downlink and 160 Gbps of uplink, with upgraded antennas, laser links and larger solar arrays. Musk said future Starship flights will carry more than 50 Tbps.

SpaceX is already looking past V3: in clips Sawyer Merritt shared, the company says it is designing a V4 satellite and that the challenge is a larger power system and better cooling. Separately, United's CEO called Starlink Wi-Fi the airline's biggest near-term advantage in its history, with nearly 600 aircraft equipped.

stories.headline: Nonprofits sue OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta and SpaceX's AI unit to stop work beyond today's frontier
stories.why_read: Courts, not Congress, may be where the first real fight over AI pause demands happens.
body: A coalition including Public Citizen, the Irreplaceable Education Fund, Heat Initiative and the Alliance for Secure AI filed suit Thursday in San Francisco Superior Court against Anthropic, Google, Meta, OpenAI and SpaceX's AI division, according to a summary of posts on X. They seek an injunction under California's Unfair Competition Law to block development of AI more powerful than current frontier models and to stop AI from directing its own research.

The complaint leans on the companies' own public warnings about loss of control, bioweapons and cyberattacks. Sen. Bernie Sanders praised the filing. Whatever happens to the injunction request, discovery fights over what the labs know internally could be the more consequential part.

stories.headline: SpaceX plans $74 billion of AI supercomputing campuses in South Texas and Arizona
stories.why_read: Power is the real constraint on AI, and these plans spell out how SpaceX intends to get it: on-site gas in Texas, solar and batteries in Arizona.
body: SpaceX is planning a $24 billion campus near Starbase and Brownsville with on-site gas power and $220 million for water infrastructure, and a $50 billion project on 747 acres in Arizona's Cochise County with up to nine buildings, according to summaries of posts on X. The Arizona site is described as needing up to 6 gigawatts and relying on solar and battery storage with minimal water use.

SpaceX is also offering about $3.6 billion in grid upgrades in Arizona that it says could lower local electricity bills. Both projects are awaiting local approvals in early December, and both put the energy question for AI training right next to Texas and Arizona communities.

stories.headline: SpaceX's AI unit reportedly cuts about 60 people from Grok Imagine to focus on coding tools and Grok Bot
stories.why_read: A clear signal of where the money is going: agents and coding, not image and video generation.
body: SpaceX's Super Intelligence unit cut roughly 60 people from the Grok Imagine image and video team last week, leaving a few to keep the tool running, according to a summary of posts on X. The resources are reportedly being moved to AI coding tools and the Grok Bot agent, following the acquisition of Cursor in August.
There was no official company statement. Grok Imagine stays available, but its future development looks uncertain as Chinese labs lead in video models.

stories.headline: Nvidia's first post since Huang's exit is GR00T 2, an open robotics model that learns from human video
stories.why_read: The roadmap keeps shipping regardless of the boardroom, and physical AI is where Nvidia wants the next platform.
body: GR00T 2 is an open robotics foundation model trained on hundreds of thousands of hours of human video that predicts the outcome of actions in the physical world, according to a summary of posts on X. It is reported to reach 95% success on new tasks after just five human demonstrations, and partners including Foxconn are testing it for factory automation.
The launch landed days after Huang stepped down, and the timing drew as much attention as the model itself.

stories.headline: Dwarkesh Patel moves his superintelligence forecast up to 2030 after AI's math run
stories.why_read: When one of the more careful long-form interviewers in AI shortens his timeline this sharply, the argument is worth reading for yourself.
body: In a new essay, Patel points to AI going from fumbling arithmetic in 2023 to solving a Millennium Prize problem in 88 hours, and argues that automated researchers could compress years of progress into months, according to a summary of posts on X. He now expects AIs to match top human researchers by 2028 and superintelligence by 2030, possibly sooner.
Skeptics note that economists credit much of the recent speedup to more human R&D spending and doubt a full self-improving loop. Either way, the essay is a clear statement of the fast-takeoff case.

stories.headline: OpenAI folds its robotics team into core research, betting general models can drive robots directly
stories.why_read: Another sign that domain-specific teams are being absorbed by frontier models.
body: OpenAI moved its standalone robotics researchers under Chief Research Officer Mark Chen and applied staff under President Greg Brockman, according to a summary of posts on X. The reasoning reported is that frontier models like GPT-6 Astra can now handle robot tasks without specialized setups.
Robotics remains part of OpenAI's plans, with a public humanoid demo reportedly planned for 2027. The change comes five months after Sam Altman publicly called for robotics hires.

stories.headline: DeepSeek exposes its consumer app's search, file parsing and voice tools through the API
stories.why_read: Building a research agent on an open-weight model just got a lot less plumbing-heavy.
body: On November 13 DeepSeek extended its app's capabilities to developers through API parameters: cited web and image search, PDF handling, automatic URL reading, and OCR, speech recognition and text-to-speech, according to a summary of posts on X. It also released an open-source frontend demo that can import conversation history.
Pricing is reported at $0.75 per 1,000 search requests, with discounts on speech features, all powered by the V4.1-Flash model.

stories.headline: Reason Machines launches a coding harness claiming frontier results at up to 20x lower cost
stories.why_read: The cost of running agents is now a competitive axis on its own, separate from which model you pick.
body: Reason launched November 13 with specialized agents for security, support and code review that run from the web, Slack, a CLI or an API and work with models such as Claude or Grok, according to a summary of posts on X. It claims frontier-level scores on Terminal-Bench and DeepSWE while cutting costs up to 20 times through prompt caching and agent specialization.
Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong reportedly merged 46 pull requests across 10 repos in 14 part-time days with it and no reverts. Plans start at $50 a month.

stories.headline: Google Antigravity's Dynamic Workflows turn a plain-English task into a reviewable Python script for subagents
stories.why_read: Making the orchestration plan an artifact you can read and approve is a sane answer to agent sprawl.
body: Announced November 13, Dynamic Workflows let you describe a task in natural language and get back a Python script using helpers like parallel() and pipeline() to coordinate subagents, according to a summary of posts on X. You approve the script before it runs in isolated chats, and reusable workflows can be saved so the main conversation stays clean.
Google reports a 19% cut in task time and 24% lower quota use on benchmarks. Varun Mohan called it a heavily used internal tool. It builds on the Orchestrator with Gemini 4 Carbon and Hydrogen.

stories.headline: A new benchmark tests whether agents in a company Slack know when to act and when to stay quiet
stories.why_read: Knowing when not to act is the skill bots in a shared workspace need most, and the models are worst at it.
body: Deepnote's Agent Initiative Benchmark drops 12 frontier models into the Slack of a synthetic company with six years of financial, CRM and ticket data and runs them through 50 realistic situations, according to a summary of posts on X. GPT-6 Astra led with 8.97 out of 10, GPT-6.1 Sol scored 8.65 and Claude Fable 5.2 scored 8.17.

Sol reportedly cost $0.11 per task versus $1.87 for Fable. Every model struggled most with holding back when no action was needed, often calling too many tools. The benchmark is open-sourced on GitHub and Hugging Face.

stories.headline: Unsloth updates its Qwen3.8-27B quants to Dynamic v3.1, claiming 5-10% better accuracy at the same size
stories.why_read: A capable 27B vision-and-reasoning model that fits in 17GB is about the sweet spot for a home GPU.
body: Qwen3.8-27B is a dense 27B model with vision and reasoning, a 256K context window, and it runs locally on setups with about 17GB of RAM or VRAM, according to Unsloth's docs. As of November 11, Unsloth's GGUFs use Dynamic V3.1, which it says improves average accuracy by 5-10% at comparable sizes on benchmarks including Terminal Bench and DeepSWE.

The model is pitched at agentic coding, vision and chat, and can be run through Unsloth's GGUFs, NVFP4 builds or the new Unsloth Desktop app. Pair it with this week's ggml 1.0 release if you serve through llama.cpp.

stories.headline: Perplexity releases Decider v1.3, an Apache-licensed classifier model for routing, judging and moderation
stories.why_read: Not every AI call needs a chatbot; a model that returns probabilities in one pass is cheaper plumbing for agents.
body: Perplexity released Decider v1.3 and a distilled Decider Flash v1.3 on Hugging Face under the Apache license, plus through OpenRouter and its Decisions API. A decision model takes an input plus a set of questions and returns a probability distribution over the answers for each, supporting yes/no, multiple choice and ordered scores in a single forward pass.

The v1.3 models add bidirectional attention, better training data and a new locate feature that highlights the selected span for entity recognition, personal data detection and extractive QA. Perplexity says it uses Decider internally for judging outputs, routing requests between model sizes and catching prompt injection in tool outputs.

stories.headline: After 600 experiments on LeCun's JEPA world model, one detail in the goal image mattered more than perfect physics
stories.why_read: A rare hands-on look at the non-generative world model debate, with a result that is both funny and instructive.
body: Haddy Alchaer spent months running 600 experiments on LeWM, a JEPA world model from a team including Yann LeCun, using the Push-T benchmark where a robot pushes a T-shaped block onto a target. JEPA models plan in embedding space instead of generating pixels: an encoder compresses each frame, a predictor forecasts the next embedding given an action, and a planner searches action sequences for the closest match to the goal.

Swapping the learned predictor for the simulator's perfect physics helped less than expected; one detail in how the goal image is presented affected success more. The post also shows how transforming a memory graph to generate subgoals on the fly lets the vanilla model solve long-horizon tasks without extra training.

stories.headline: Meta extends LLDB to debug programs that span CPUs and GPUs in one session
stories.why_read: AI workloads bounce between host code and GPU kernels, and until now debugging across that line meant vendor-specific tools.
body: Meta engineers built a vendor-neutral accelerator plugin architecture in lldb-server that represents the CPU and GPU as separate debugger processes but shows them in one debugging session. Shared debugger infrastructure stays independent of any single GPU, while hardware vendors implement device-specific control in a focused plugin.

The post explains why GPUs break the classic debugger model: different instruction sets, separate address spaces and thousands of lanes running in lockstep. It contrasts the approach with vendor tools such as ROCgdb and CUDA-GDB, which have to re-implement common debugger features on their own.

stories.headline: Reverse engineering a Coway air purifier to cut out the cloud
stories.why_read: Classic IoT frustration turned into a satisfying local-control hack, the kind your homelab would appreciate.
body: Scott's Coway Airmega IconS could only be controlled through Coway's cloud: the Home Assistant integration polls Coway's servers and sends commands through them, and the phone app is slow and keeps asking for a password change. He wanted the fan to ramp up to white-noise level when he pressed an Apple Home "Good Night" scene.

The write-up walks through reverse engineering the device so it can be controlled on the local network without the round trip through Coway's servers, which is a useful template for any appliance with a lazy cloud dependency.

stories.headline: Ratatui's maintainer proposes terminal borders that are drawn on cell edges instead of costing a row and column
stories.why_read: A small protocol idea that could make TUIs look much less boxy, and it is asking for feedback from terminal authors.
body: The maintainer of Ratatui is prototyping a terminal protocol that draws thin lines on the edges of cells rather than using box-drawing characters. He has it working as a patch to Ghostty, with an earlier version in Rio, and built Ratatui demo apps for it.

With cell borders, panes keep every row and column, tab labels sit on a pane's top edge, text fields get an underline right under the text, and buttons can be one row tall and rounded. In terminals without support, the demo falls back to box-drawing characters, and each pane loses a row and column on every side.

stories.headline: FreeBSD's bhyve gets a working live-migration prototype on 15.1
stories.why_read: Live migration is the missing piece for running FreeBSD as a serious Proxmox-style virtualization host.
body: A work-in-progress RFC shows a running amd64 bhyve guest moving between two FreeBSD 15.1 hosts over TCP while it keeps running, paused only for the final stop-and-copy phase. It builds on bhyve's experimental snapshot support, adding dirty-page tracking to the vmm kernel module and a migration protocol in bhyve and bhyvectl.

The pre-copy phase sends guest memory, then repeatedly sends only pages dirtied since the last scan until the remainder fits the downtime target. The author wants it for the Sylve virtualization project and his free BoxyBSD VPS service, and published the code so the next steps can be shaped in the open.

stories.headline: Tesla's AI chief: self-driving watches all 360 degrees and can move you out of danger from any direction
stories.why_read: A short post you bookmarked that captures the core safety argument for camera-based autonomy.
body: Ashok Elluswamy, who leads Tesla's AI and Autopilot software, posted that Tesla's self-driving system monitors all 360 degrees around the car at once and can steer you out of danger coming from any direction.
It lands the same week Tesla opened Cybercab orders, a car that depends entirely on that system because it has no steering wheel or pedals for a human to take over.

stories.headline: Researchers find an enzyme that drives tissue ageing, and blocking it may not weaken immune defenses
stories.why_read: Most anti-ageing targets come with immune trade-offs; this one may not, at least in mice.
body: Researchers have identified an enzyme that drives ageing in the body's tissues, Nature reports, in a study published in Immunity by Kannangara and colleagues. Mice bioengineered to lack the enzyme showed less age-related stiffening and scarring of liver tissue.

The hope is that drugs reducing levels of this protein could one day counter some effects of ageing without impairing the body's immune defenses, which many inflammation-focused approaches risk doing. It is early, mouse-stage work.

stories.headline: A 12-year study finds Sri Lanka's Asian elephants slipping past a social tipping point
stories.why_read: A sobering, beautifully observed study about what happens to a close-knit society when it slowly loses members.
body: UC San Diego researchers tracked more than 440 wild female Asian elephants over 12 years in Udawalawe National Park, and their study is on the cover of the November 12 issue of Science. They found that a gradual accumulation of losses from population turnover came before a sudden change in social networks, leaving communities smaller and more isolated.

The team, led by postdoctoral researcher Anastasia Madsen in Shermin de Silva's lab, warns that crossing such a tipping point can harm the animals' future, since elephants rely on group bonds to find food and raise their young.

stories.headline: DeepMind releases open datasets for global 15-minute rainfall and hourly cloud maps
stories.why_read: Better cloud and rain data means better solar forecasts and flood warnings, especially where there is no radar.
body: Google DeepMind released PARDIG, which provides global rainfall estimates every 15 minutes and improves detection by more than 30% over existing tools, and SatWeave, which stitches satellite views into hourly global cloud maps, according to a summary of posts on X.

Both come with years of historical data plus real-time streams on Google Cloud and Earth Engine, aimed at flood warnings, wildfire tracking, solar energy forecasting and training better weather models.

stories.headline: Lonewolf 0.3, a standalone XMPP server in Rust, adds federation and direct TLS
stories.why_read: Open, federated chat you can run yourself keeps getting easier to deploy.
body: Lonewolf 0.3 lets users exchange messages, presence and roster subscriptions with people on other XMPP servers. Federation is on by default when a host has a certificate and public DNS name, peers are authenticated by certificate only, and the release adds direct TLS from the first byte plus private XML storage and software-version support for desktop clients.
It is still pre-1.0 and single-node, with full XMPP compliance and clustering on the roadmap.

stories.headline: ULA's Vulcan return to flight slips a day after a power glitch at a nitrogen plant
stories.why_read: A reminder that launch readiness depends on ground infrastructure as much as the rocket.
body: United Launch Alliance scrubbed Friday's Vulcan launch from Cape Canaveral after a power interruption disabled high-pressure pumps at the Air Liquide gaseous nitrogen facility, according to a summary of posts on X. The rocket and its 40 Amazon Leo satellites were healthy, and the launch was reset for Saturday, November 14, at 12:32:30 p.m. EST.
It is Vulcan's first flight in nine months, since a booster nozzle problem in February, and features six solid rocket boosters and a redesigned nozzle.
